justice: The street allocates substantial space to multiple users through a broad roadway, a planted central median, and a separate sidewalk zone on the right side.
Accessibility is only moderate because no curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free details are visible in this scene.
Fairness across modes appears uneven since motor vehicles have clearly defined travel lanes, while no dedicated bicycle lane is visible for cyclists.
The continuous sidewalk on the right suggests some provision for pedestrians, but the left side appears dominated by landscaping rather than an accessible walking edge.
safety: The central planted median and hedge buffer help separate opposing traffic flows and reduce the chance of head-on conflicts.
Streetlights are installed regularly along both sides, supporting baseline nighttime visibility and perceived security.
The road is wide and visually clear with long sightlines, which improves forward visibility for drivers and helps all users anticipate movements.
Safety is reduced for non-motorized users because no marked bike lane, crossing markings, or traffic-calming features are visible on this segment.
livability: Dense rows of mature trees and hedges create a green corridor that improves environmental quality and makes the street more pleasant.
Livability is limited by the absence of visible shops, seating, transit stops, or active public-frontage uses that would support daily social activity.
The setting appears quiet and orderly, with low visible congestion and a clean roadway surface, which supports a calm urban environment.
Large setbacks and a car-oriented street profile make the space feel more like a through-road than a socially active neighborhood street.
sustainability: Extensive street trees and continuous planted hedges provide urban greening, shade, and likely heat-mitigation benefits.
The vegetated median and roadside planting strips indicate investment in green infrastructure rather than a fully paved corridor.
The long, straight corridor with generous planting can support better air-quality buffering between traffic and sidewalks.
Sustainability is constrained by the lack of visible public transit facilities or dedicated cycling infrastructure that would more strongly support low-carbon travel.
aesthetics: The avenue has strong visual coherence, with repeated streetlights, aligned tree rows, and continuous hedges creating an orderly composition.
Mature greenery on both sides and in the median gives the corridor a lush and visually attractive character.
The street appears clean and well maintained, with neat planting edges and an uncluttered roadway.
The open sky view and long perspective enhance the boulevard-like appearance and make the scene visually expansive.
comfort: Thermal comfort is relatively good because tall street trees provide substantial shade over the sidewalk and part of the roadside edge.
Physical comfort is supported by a smooth road surface and a continuous sidewalk on the right with a planted buffer from traffic.
Psychological comfort benefits from the green enclosure created by trees and hedges, which softens the otherwise wide vehicular corridor.
Comfort is reduced somewhat because no benches, shelters, or visible resting amenities are present for people spending time on foot.
walkability: A continuous sidewalk is visible on the right side, separated from the roadway by hedges and trees, which supports pedestrian movement.
Shade from the mature trees improves walking conditions, especially in sunny weather.
Walkability is limited because no crosswalks, pedestrian signals, curb ramps, or destination-oriented frontage are visible in this segment.
The wide road and sparse visible pedestrian activity make the corridor feel more optimized for movement through the area than for walking-oriented street life.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane, painted cycle markings, or physically protected cycling space is visible on the roadway.
The broad carriageway may allow cycling in mixed traffic, but the absence of separation lowers comfort and perceived safety for most riders.
The planted median and roadside hedges improve the corridor environment, yet they do not substitute for actual cycling infrastructure.
No bicycle parking, bike boxes, or intersection treatments are visible, so cycling convenience appears limited.
